newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK housing woes a hot potato for future leader Tung.
newsitem.headline: HK housing woes a hot potato for future leader Tung.

text.p: Hong Kong's housing problem is fast becoming a political hot potato that will test the territory's post-colonial leaders after China takes over in July, political experts and analysts said on Thursday.

"This will become a very politically explosive issue. If the future Hong Kong SAR government cannot handle it skillfully and successfully...it will undermine its legitimacy," analyst Sonny Lo, a researcher on the Hong Kong 1997 transition, told Reuters.

From July 1, Hong Kong will no longer be a British crown colony but a special administrative region (SAR) of China, run by its chief executive, Tung Chee-hwa, a billionaire shipping magnate carefully chosen by Beijing.

While Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule has been rocked by political debates, spiralling property prices have stolen centre stage most recently, with irate residents planting a fake bomb outside the legislature and posting a death threat letter to the territory's housing chief.
In the affluent territory of 6.4 million people, which boasts some HK$330 billion (US$42.7 billion) in reserves, many working adults still cannot afford to buy their own homes.

Under public fire, the present colonial government has promised to increase land supply for residential use and raise flat supply to 22,000 units in 1997 and 36,000 in 1998, which it says will help meet average demand of 25,000 units each year.
Tung has recognised the magnitude of the problem and pledged to make housing his top priority. But this makes him vulnerable.
"If Tung Chee-hwa solves the problem, it will give him prestige and great political clout.

"But if not, people will lose confidence, feel let down, and this will aggravate the level of discontent and even (produce) a sense of betrayal," said Lau Siu-kai, a professor and pro-China politician at The Chinese University of Hong Kong.
"His government will be in trouble," Lau, who is a member of China-controlled handover institutions, told Reuters.
Another academic, who declined to be named, said Tung faced a difficult dilemma over the property sector, one of the main engines of Hong Kong's bustling economy and stock market.
"He wants to bring down the housing prices, but if there is a crash, there could be a major recession. I don't think he wants to see that in the first year of his rule," he said.
The issue snowballed last month when Tung appointed Leung Chun-ying -- a prominent pro-China politician and real estate tycoon -- as post-colonial housing troubleshooter.
Critics and the public saw in this a conflict of interest. Radio chat shows were swamped with calls slamming Tung's move as evidence that politicians were in cahoots with business.
This week, six companies advertised in newspapers to announce that Leung had resigned directorships with them. But the damage has been done, analysts said.
"His withdrawal from some of the major companies cannot calm anxiety because the public seems to have the view that the government is collaborating with business people," Lo said.
Beijing is obviously worried by the problem.
"Beijing has been paying close attention to this problem. After all, if Hong Kong has social problems after the transition it will be a loss of face," academic Lau said.
Some thought escalation of the problem might even force Beijing to step into the fray after Hong Kong's handover.

"After July 1, the central government in Beijing will take an interest in this issue," Lo said. "Chinese officials will through official or informal channels, inform the future leadership more should be done to deal with the problem."
